phonemes.desc: Voiceless labiodental fricative [f] plus [j], the palatal glide that begins the name.
Short open-mid rounded vowel [ɒ] plus [r], a Norse vowel distinctive to the tradition.
Voiced [g] plus short [y] and [n], the feminine ending related to the same element seen in Jǫrð.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FYOR-guin' — the first syllable carries the stress; the final syllable has a rounded 'u' sound followed by a light 'n'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Fjǫrgyn, the goddess or earth-personification, mother of Þórr

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Possibly related to Old Norse fjor, "life, vital force," or to a word for "fir/tree"; the exact origin is debated

kin.label: Variant
kin.form: Fjǫrgynn, the masculine form applied to a male deity or giant in some sources

pronunciation.note: Fjǫrgyn is Tier 1 because the restored form preserves the distinctive ǫ and the final gy — features the ASCII form fjorgyn loses.

domains.title: Earth and Mother of Thor
domains.subtitle: The Land That Brings Forth
domains.lead: Fjǫrgyn is one of the names by which the Norse earth appears as a goddess. She is the mother of Þórr, the thunder-god, and in the sources she is invoked as the ground that receives oaths, the field that bears grain, and the ancient power beneath every footstep. Whether she is a distinct goddess or another name for Jǫrð is debated, but her name carries its own resonance: life, oak, and the green world.

cards.name: Mother of Thor
cards.desc: The Poetic Edda names Fjǫrgyn as the mother of Þórr, linking the thunder-god to the earth itself.

cards.name: Lady of the Fir and Oak
cards.desc: Her name may connect to words for tree and life; she is the green force that supports the world-tree.

cards.name: Earth Personified
cards.desc: Like Jǫrð, she is the land invoked in oaths and the ground that endures storm and war.

cards.name: Witness of Oaths
cards.desc: Lokasenna invokes Fjǫrgyn as the earth beneath, the silent witness to sworn words.

symbols.name: The fertile field
symbols.meaning: The earth that bears crops and supports the weight of gods and men

symbols.name: Oak or fir
symbols.meaning: The tree of life connected to her name and to Þórr's lightning

symbols.name: The oath-ring or stone
symbols.meaning: The earth invoked as witness to binding vows

symbols.name: Thor's hammer
symbols.meaning: The weapon of the son she bore to Óðinn

mythology.lead: Fjǫrgyn appears briefly in the Eddas, but her appearances are weighty: she is the mother of the most popular god and the earth that hears every oath.

myths.title: The Earth as Insult
myths.text: In the flyting of Lokasenna, Loki turns on Sif and then on Þórr, boasting of his own encounters. Þórr threatens Loki, who answers mockingly. The poem earlier names Fjǫrgyn as Þórr's mother, making the thunder-god the son of the earth — a fitting parent for a deity whose realm is the storm above the fields.

myths.title: Among the Earth-Kennings
myths.text: Snorri lists Fjǫrgyn among the names and kennings for the earth. She is 'Mother of Þórr,' 'Wife of Óðinn,' and 'Daughter of Annarr.' The prose tradition treats her as closely identified with Jǫrð, perhaps as a poetic byname or perhaps as a separate figure absorbed into the larger conception of the earth-goddess.

myths.title: Life and Tree
myths.text: Scholars debate whether Fjǫrgyn derives from a root meaning "life" (fjor) or "tree" (fura, "fir"). Either etymology deepens her character: she is the living earth or the forested earth, the green substrate of the Norse cosmos. The masculine form Fjǫrgynn, applied to a giant or to Óðinn himself in some sources, suggests the name belongs to an old divine family of which the earth-goddess is one branch.

lore.syncretism: Fjǫrgyn is almost certainly the same figure as Jǫrð under a different name, or a closely related byname of the Norse earth-goddess. The pairing of sky-god and earth-goddess — Óðinn with Fjǫrgyn/Jǫrð — is an Indo-European commonplace, parallel to Zeús and Gaîa/Gē, the Vedic Dyáuṣ and Pṛthivī, and the Irish Donn and the land. In later Scandinavian folklore, the earth continued to be invoked in oaths and childbirth, preserving the old goddess under the name of the land itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fjǫrgyn survives chiefly as a name in handbooks of Norse mythology and in poetic lists of the earth. Modern Heathen practice sometimes distinguishes her from Jǫrð as a more forested or vital aspect of the land, while scholars generally treat her as a byname. Her importance lies in her son: every invocation of Þórr as "Fjǫrgyn's son" remembers that the thunderer is born of the earth. Restoring Fjǫrgyn keeps the ǫ and the gy that mark the name as Old Norse, not modern Scandinavian.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Fjǫrgyn is the earth under another name — or perhaps the earth in one of her moods. Where Jǫrð is the broad land, Fjǫrgyn may be the living, tree-bearing, oath-witnessing earth. She is mother to the storm, and that pairing is one of the oldest images in Indo-European religion: the sky meets the land, and from their union comes the god who protects both.

To speak her name is to remember that the ground is not dead matter. It hears oaths. It brings forth grain and oak. It endures. In an age that often treats the earth as a resource, Fjǫrgyn is the old voice that says the land has always been a goddess, and that divinity is owed to the soil beneath our feet.

lore.archaeology: Fjǫrgyn is a textual figure with no independent archaeological record. No inscription names her, and no image can be securely identified with her. Her witnesses are the Eddic poems and Snorri's Prose Edda, supported by the wider Germanic and Indo-European pattern of an earth-goddess paired with a sky-god.
